blocks.title: Isomers
blocks.text: Two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but a different arrangement of atoms and different properties are isomers; the phenomenon is isomerism.

items: When the same atoms or groups are joined at different places, the result is structural (constitutional) isomerism: chain, position and functional group isomers, metamers and tautomers, studied in Chemistry XI.
When the atoms are joined in the same order but arranged differently in space (a different configuration), the result is stereoisomerism.

blocks.alt: A chart. Isomers (same molecular formula) divide into constitutional or structural isomers (chain, position, functional group, metamers, tautomers) and stereoisomers. Stereoisomers divide into conformational (interconvert by rotation about single bonds) and configurational; configurational into optical isomers and geometrical (cis-trans, restricted rotation about C=C); optical isomers into enantiomers (non-superimposable mirror images) and diastereomers (not mirror images).
blocks.caption: Classification of isomers (original chart after the book's scheme).
blocks.long_description: Isomers first divide by whether their atoms are joined in the same order. Constitutional isomers have different connections. Stereoisomers have the same connections but a different arrangement in space: conformational isomers change into one another just by rotation about single bonds, while configurational isomers, optical or geometrical, cannot change without breaking bonds.
